## Categorizing open-end survey responses is slow, manual, and inconsistent at scale {.paper}

::: {.eyebrow}
WHY ORCA EXISTS
:::

[AI can accelerate the work of categorizing thousands of free-text answers. But for a research firm's internal stakeholders and clients, speed means nothing without trust in the result.]{.lede .mt-md}

::: {.chips .mt-lg}
[Transparency]{.chip}
[Trust]{.chip}
[Reproducibility]{.chip}
:::

::: notes
**Michael**:

In just a moment, Keaton is going to talk about "open-end survey coding". But when we say *coding*, we don't mean R or Python code -- we're talking about taking free-text data from user surveys and tagging them as belonging to one of many possible fixed categories. You might be able to think of it along the same lines as sentiment analysis, but instead of measuring how positive or negative the sentiment in a paragraph of text is, we're instead wanting to *categorize* what that paragraph of text is talking about -- and assigning it to a single pre-defined category.

**Keaton**:

- slow and manual process, lots of human time.
- also be *inconsistent* at scale.
- The team at KS&R had a hypothesis that AI could accelerate this task — but we knew that internal stakeholders and clients would not accept a "black box" doing this work.
:::

## One system, two companies {.cream}

::: {.eyebrow}
A CROSS-COMPANY BUILD
:::

[Built as one of KS&R's DS&I project teams — a research firm and an external consultancy, one shared build.]{.cap .mt-sm}

::::: {.versus .fill .mt-md}
:::: {.card .centered}
![](images/ksr-logo.png){.logo-xl}

::: foot
[Research firm — backend & infrastructure owner]{.cap}
:::
::::
::: glyph
\+
:::
:::: {.card .centered}
![](images/ketchbrook-mark.png){.logo-lg}

![](images/ketchbrook-wordmark.png){.logo-md}

::: foot
[Consultancy — front-end & UX owner]{.cap}
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.kicker}
Why not in-house? A one-developer team, several competing priorities, and a lift that needed to happen **now**.
:::

::: notes
*Michael*
The work to build this solution was very explicitly divided: KS&R owned the back-end, server-side code, and the front-end user interface was Ketchbrook's responsibility.

Maybe this sounds scary, but there are some obvious benefits to this:

- Speed: if you can truly work in parallel, obviously two people working simultaneously will get the job done faster than one
- Error catching: more eyes on the code is more likely to catch issues
- Diversity of thought: the best ideas will prevail (as opposed to only one person's idea)
- Specialization: no one individual person has to be a jack-of-all-trades — people can focus on what they're best at

~~In our case, there were even some other additional benefits:~~

Here's how we rationalized dividing up the work in this particular case. We're not necessarily advocating for this exact delegation strategy -- you may find in your own projects that separating the work between multiple parties works better by delegating different pages of an app to different developers, adopting our front end vs. back end strategy, or something totally different. Just make sure the split it is *well-defined*.

KS&R found that the front-end/back-end delegation led to lower institutional and financial risk for an external partner -- like Ketchbrook -- to touch the AI-spend involved.

And from our perspective, we *prefer* to not have to hold on to our clients' API keys or sensitive data so that we don't have to deal with the responsibility of securing that -- the best security posture is having nothing sensitive to secure in the first place.

*Keaton*
- One developer call out. We weren't missing skills in-house, but we were missing bandwidth. The team at KS&R was already stretched across several competing priorities, and this lift needed to happen *now*.

~~Feedback: Have Keaton talk about *why* KS&R sought out an external collaborator as opposed to just doing it themselves in-house.~~ (addressed)
:::

::: notes
**Keaton**:
The architecture that made this possible. Focus on the top row: a golem-based Shiny app decoupled from a plumber API for async job processing, so the UI could be built and iterated against a stable API surface while the heavier AI/coding logic evolved behind it. ORCAstra is what actually talks to the OpenAI batch API — the front end never holds a key.

Don't dwell on the greyed pieces — just name them so the shape is on screen: ORCAdb is a pins board on Connect holding batch metadata and run history; ORCAwatch is a scheduled Quarto document that polls ORCAstra for finished jobs, reads and updates that pin, and writes the cleaned files out to the network share, then emails the submitter once delivery is complete. We come back to both in chapter 3.
:::

## One workflow, two contracts {.cream}

::: {.eyebrow}
THE KEY MOVE
:::

:::: {.split .split-even .fill .mt-md}
::: col

:::

::: notes
**Michael**:

Now we're moving from pure UI design and styling into thinking about UX.

Having a clear sense ("contracts") of what the incoming data is going to look like is critical to buildling a UI that supports the actual user workflow, accomplishes what KS&R was looking for from an expected UX.

Also having well-defined contracts of what the *outgoing* data should look like (i.e., the data going to the back-end API that Keaton was developing) ensured that we were setting him up for success.

These contracts also helped us "defensively program" against anything that would *break* that contract, and allow us to point users back in the right direction as opposed to giving them a "Server disconnected" error message and the app shutting down.

The big picture here -- neither KS&R nor Ketchbrook were every guessing at or assuming the other's needs.
:::

## Tips for a successful Design phase {.paper}

::: {.eyebrow}
TAKEAWAY — BEFORE YOU BUILD
:::

::: {.bullets .lg .mt-lg}
- Before your next cross-team project starts, get both sides in front of **one shared visual artifact** — Mural, Excalidraw, a whiteboard photo. Not a spec document.
- Argue about it there, while changing it costs nothing. Every disagreement you surface on the wireframe is one you don't discover in a pull request three weeks later.
:::

::: notes
Michael, active takeaway for chapter 1: the thing to actually do on Monday is get a shared visual artifact in front of both teams before anyone opens an editor. Cheap to change, and it forces the disagreements out early.

You may not catch *everything* here -- smaller things may come up as you actually go from 2D static design document to a living, breathing app... **but** this will help expedite so many of those future nitpicks and the major concepts will be agreed upon up front.
:::

## Issues and PRs as the shared source of truth {.paper}

::: {.eyebrow}
WORKING ASYNC, ACROSS COMPANIES
:::

:::: {.cols-2 .mt-lg}
::: col
[GitHub Issues tracked what needed to happen and who owned it — across two companies, with no shared Slack or shared employer.]{.lede}
:::
::: col
[A branching model let each side ship independently against the agreed contract, and merge without stepping on the other's work.]{.lede}
:::
::::

::: notes
**Michael**:

Communication can be tricky when you're collaborating across different organizations like we were. Communicating within Microsoft Teams or Slack might not always be possible depending on your IT teams' posture/infrastructure/security. And email is an extremely inefficient way to program together.

We needed a communication vehicle that would allow us to not only check in with each other and provide project status updates, but could also serve as a task-oriented tool that would hold us both accountable and provide a single source of truth. GitHub Branches, Issues and PRs fit that mold perfectly, allowing us to see each other's progress and work asynchronously without impeding one another.
:::

## Not an assertion — **receipts.** {.navy .statement}

[Issues, PRs, and a contract everyone could point to — that's why this collaboration held together.]{.lede}

## Make the issue the interface {.paper}

::: {.eyebrow}
TAKEAWAY — WHILE YOU BUILD
:::

::: {.bullets .lg .mt-lg}
- Write Issues and PR bodies for **someone who doesn't share your codebase, your standup, or your employer**. Detail that feels excessive inside one team is the bare minimum across two.
- If a decision only exists in a call or a DM, it doesn't exist. Put it where the other company can find it without asking you.
:::

Next — Keaton, on earning trust in production →
:::

::: notes
Michael, active takeaway for chapter 2: over-document across the boundary. The written trail is what let us work in parallel without blocking each other — and it's the habit that transfers to any partner team.

Blythe's test: would we have designed it this way even if it weren't an AI app? Yes — which is exactly the point.

::: notes
Keaton: modularizing the backend independently from the front end is what made the parallel, non-blocking collaboration possible. Four pieces, each with one job.

ORCA — Michael's side. Worth naming brand.yml here: KS&R's brand book went in as a config file, so the app picked up our colours and type without anyone hand-porting them. That's the constraints-as-a-gift slide paying off in practice.

ORCAstra — the plumber point is the one to land: we built a well-defined surface for each core function and hosted them internally, so the front end could call a stable endpoint while everything behind it kept changing. It leans on ksRAI, an internal R package we wrote to make interfacing with the OpenAI API straightforward — cost estimation, batch submission, response parsing — so that logic lives in one tested place instead of being scattered through the API.

ORCAdb — pins on Connect for versioned metadata and run history.

ORCAwatch — a scheduled Quarto document on Connect. purrr is not decoration here: the batch API returns deeply nested lists, and the shape of the coding data is nested too, so the whole wrangling step is map/pluck work.
:::

## Build a seam, not a handoff {.paper}

::: {.eyebrow}
TAKEAWAY — AFTER YOU SHIP
:::

::: {.bullets .lg .mt-lg}
- Pick the boundary between the two teams **deliberately**, then make it something both sides can build against without waiting — an API, a versioned artifact, a pinned dataset.
- A good seam means either side can be replaced, rewritten, or handed to someone new without renegotiating the whole system. That's what makes the collaboration outlast the project.
:::

::: notes
Keaton, active takeaway for chapter 3: the architecture is what lets the collaboration survive. Choose the seam on purpose, make it stable, and both sides stay unblocked long after the initial build.
:::

Through rigorous wireframing, providing style guides up front, using issues/branches/PRs to strongly document, delegate, and isolate your work 

Michael: the real product wasn't just ORCA — it was a repeatable model for cross-company, cross-discipline collaboration on the Posit stack.
:::

## Bring a design artifact to your next cross-team project — not just code {.paper}

::: {.eyebrow}
IF YOU'RE BUILDING WITH A PARTNER TEAM
:::

:::: {.cols-3 .mt-lg}
::: {.card .cream}
A shared visual contract — Mural, Excalidraw, or a whiteboard, before anyone opens an editor.
:::
::: {.card .cream}
Issue-driven development — a shared source of truth across company lines. Don't skimp on detail in your Issues & PR bodies.
:::
::: {.card .cream}
An architecture — [golem]{.pkg} + [plumber]{.pkg} + [pins]{.pkg} — that lets both sides move independently.
:::
::::

::: notes
Michael: if you're building Shiny apps with a partner team — agency/client, research/engineering, frontend/backend — invest early in shared visual contracts, issue-driven development, and an architecture that lets both sides move independently against a stable interface.
:::
